Chapter 2: Identifying the Subtle Signs and Tactics of Covert Abuse
Now that you’ve got a sense of how covert narcissism works behind the scenes, let’s dive into how you can actually spot the tactics in real life. The tricky part? These behaviors are so subtle, they often look like normal relationship ups and downs—or might even come across as caring. But, over time, they leave you feeling confused, second-guessing yourself, and just plain worn out.
One of the biggest red flags is gaslighting. Have you ever found yourself questioning your own memory or wondering if you’re just imagining things? That’s what gaslighting does. Someone might deny ever saying something hurtful, insist an event never happened, or brush you off as being “too sensitive.” It’s a slow drip—before you know it, you’re doubting your own reality and struggling to trust your instincts.
Another common move is emotional withdrawal. Rather than getting into open arguments, a covert narcissist might just pull away. Maybe it’s the silent treatment, withholding affection, or becoming emotionally distant. You’re left feeling insecure, wondering what you did wrong, and often trying even harder to win back their approval.
Passive-aggressive behaviors show up a lot, too. Think of things like procrastinating on purpose, “forgetting” important dates, or not following through on promises. Sometimes, it’s those little digs—like a dismissive comment that undermines your achievements. These actions are meant to frustrate you and keep you off-balance, but if you call them out, there’s always a way for them to deny it.
Playing the victim is another classic tactic. You might notice they always seem misunderstood, mistreated, or unappreciated. It’s a way to get sympathy and shift the blame onto you or others, all while drawing in the attention and validation they crave.
Then there’s triangulation. This is when they pull a third person into the mix—maybe by comparing you to someone else, or by using others to deliver messages. Suddenly, you’re competing for their attention or feeling jealous, and the focus is all about regaining their approval.
Here’s the thing: these aren’t just one-off incidents. They form a pattern—a constant sense that you’re walking on eggshells, always anxious about what might spark the next round of withdrawal or criticism.
So, why does all this matter? Because recognizing these patterns is the first real step toward taking back your sense of what’s real. It helps you separate normal relationship bumps from the calculated, repeated behaviors that define covert abuse. That clarity? It’s the foundation you need to start setting boundaries and reclaiming your confidence.
